# Reflection & Learnings

## Challenges & Lessons Learned

Since we did not have access to real customer data, we worked with synthetic data that we created ourselves. The tariff data, however, is based on real information and consists of 62 documents containing published provider pricing. We created the ten customer personas, their subscriptions, and roughly two thousand synthetic trip legs. The travel histories had to be sufficiently varied to make the recommendations meaningful, as perfectly regular travel patterns would make most cases too simple. But it also means we were marking our own homework. The engine prices real tariffs correctly against behaviour we designed, and we have no way of knowing how it behaves against a real customer who takes an unexplained Uber every third Friday. The provider connection step in the onboarding is simulated for the same reason. We designed the interaction as though it were real, which we think is the right way round: the pattern is testable now, and only the data source would need replacing.

Our work was organised around a weekly meeting every Wednesday, where we discussed the progress from the previous week and agreed on the next tasks. Implementation was mostly carried out individually or in pairs, particularly during the weekends. With five team members and different schedules, this worked better than trying to coordinate continuously. The main disadvantage was that problems arising during the weekend sometimes had to wait until the following meeting. We used a GitHub repository with defined areas of responsibility and a Notion workspace for planning, which helped keep the work organised and reduced conflicts.

The final weeks of the project overlapped with the examination period for all five team members. Although this made the final phase more demanding, most of the implementation had already been completed. The remaining work mainly involved integration, testing, and writing. In retrospect, the lesson is to complete the work that requires sustained concentration before the schedule becomes crowded, since the tasks that can still be handled reliably under time pressure are the smaller ones.

## Limitations & Next Steps

The tariff data represents a snapshot and does not currently include a mechanism for updating prices when provider conditions change. The customer data is synthetic, so the evaluation does not show how the recommendations would perform with real-world travel behaviour. The provider connection during onboarding is also simulated rather than integrated with an actual provider.

Another limitation concerns the transport data used for alternatives that the customer did not actually use. CO~2~ emissions and travel duration are based on manually defined averages rather than route-specific data. The multi-criteria scoring is also limited by the structure of the problem itself. Within a single category the alternatives do not change how a person travels, so emissions and duration are identical across them and the decision is effectively made on cost. The CO~2~ and flexibility weights only become decisive when the system compares different modes of transport. In addition to that, the system currently considers one person at a time and therefore does not support shared household arrangements or employer-funded mobility.

Future work could address these limitations in several ways. A real OAuth-based provider connection, starting with the Deutschlandticket, would allow the system to work with actual travel data. Adding route-level emissions and duration data from a routing service would give the CO~2~ and time axes enough resolution to actually change a recommendation, which the manually defined averages cannot. Finally, extending the evaluation from a single analysis run to rolling time windows would test the claim the product is built on, namely that the advice stays correct as someone's behaviour changes. None of these require redesigning anything: the tariff knowledge base is file-driven, and the scoring engine takes its weights as parameters rather than hard-coding them.
